newsitem.title: MEXICO: JUNE TRADE DATA SPIKE SURPRISES MEXICO ECONOMISTS.
newsitem.headline: JUNE TRADE DATA SPIKE SURPRISES MEXICO ECONOMISTS.

text.p: An upward spike in Mexico's June trade surplus, where most analysts had expected a figure headed towards a deficit, suggests the country may move into the red later than expected, some economists say.
Mexico's Finance Ministry published revised June data late on Thursday showing a trade surplus of $308 million, stronger even than May's upwardly revised surplus of $220 million.
A Reuter survey of analysts' forecasts originally showed an average expectation of $164.83 million for June.
"(Thursday's number) was almost double what the market had expected. Exports outperformed expectations," Frank Gill, Latin America analyst at I.D.E.A., said on Friday.

Added Bankers Trust economist Denis Parisien: "We had expected the number to be shifting closer to zero on its way to a deficit. The size of the surplus certainly was a positive surprise. It is largely a result of stronger than expected export performance."
Many economists expected exports to suffer from a peso that refuses to budge from its current strong levels, but other factors are off-setting the currency drag.
ING Barings economist Sergio Martin said Mexican goods remained competitive despite the strong peso because Mexican wage costs were still low and productivity robust.
The strength of the U.S. economy, which absorbs the lion's share of Mexican exports, was also of vital importance.
"It's the strength of U.S. demand more than the peso," Parisien said.
But he added that June's number suggested Mexico's projected trade deficit might come a couple of months later than previously thought.
"A lot of people were thinking it would come in the third quarter, but we now think it will be the fourth quarter," he said. "Mexico is moving towards a deficit -- it can't be avoided."
Martin was struck more by the expansion in imports in June than the robust export picture.
Capital goods rose 47.6 percent month on month and consumer goods rose nearly 60 percent, albeit from June 1996's very low base.

"Imports grew very fast in June, up nearly 33 percent. That is very rapid and a much higher figure than (we have seen) recently," he said. "The situation is that we are on our way to a trade deficit."
But he forecast that the deficit would arrive sooner than Parisien forecast.
"The fact is that we are being very much affected by the strong peso also on the import side," Martin said.
"We will have a deficit in August or September, but it will not be because of exports but because of imports," he said.
